summary: A 1975 note about the problem of junk mail on the ARPANET, unwanted messages that fill up users' mailboxes. It is an early discussion of what we now call spam.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 706 points out that a host could not ask the ARPA Network to block messages from a particular source. It proposes letting a host request that its IMP refuse those messages.

questions: how could a host refuse unwanted messages
subtitle: A short proposal for refusing unwanted messages at the Host/IMP interface.

tldr.problem: The ARPA Network Host/IMP interface had no way for a host to selectively refuse incoming messages, so a malfunctioning sender could consume processing time and network capacity.
tldr.mechanism: A host could ask its IMP to refuse messages from a named host. The destination IMP could filter them itself or pass the refusal to the source IMP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents selective message refusal as a useful interface capability and leaves the implementation approach open.

today: RFC 706 is a proposal about selective message refusal at the ARPA Network Host/IMP interface. It explicitly leaves the way IMPs would implement the capability as an open issue.

sections.title: The Problem of Unwanted Messages
sections.content:
The Host/IMP interface protocol had no mechanism for a host to selectively refuse messages. A host that wanted particular messages therefore had to read all messages addressed to it.

A malfunctioning host could send many unwanted messages, consuming processing time and network capacity and delaying other traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A host had to receive and examine messages even when they were unwanted. A malfunctioning sender could make that work consume resources.

sections.title: Refusing a Source Host
sections.content:
The memo proposes that a host be able to tell its IMP, “refuse messages from Host X.” The IMPs could discard those messages as early as possible and return a refusal notice to the sending host.

One option is for the destination IMP to keep a list of sources to refuse for each local host. Another is for it to forward the request to the source IMP, which keeps a list of refusing destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: A host could name a source whose messages should be refused. The IMP could keep that rule locally or send the rule to the source host's IMP.

sections.title: Changing or Removing a Refusal
sections.content:
The proposed restriction could be removed by a host sending an “accept messages from Host X” message to its IMP. Resetting the Host/IMP interface could also remove it.

A host might count unwanted messages from each source and issue a refusal request when a chosen threshold is exceeded. The RFC leaves the details of how IMPs would implement the feature open.
sections.plainLanguage: A host could later allow messages from that source again. It might base a refusal on how many unwanted messages arrive.
